profile.feeling: Warm and universal — the safe “hello” for anyone, anywhere, any time of day.

examples.tr: Hello! How are you? (to a man)
Welcome to our home. (to a man)

collocations.tr: welcome (to a man / a woman / several people)

synonyms.nuance: peace be upon you — the greeting everybody uses, also in formal and religious settings

etymology.text: Related to the verb رَحِبَ (raḥiba, “to be wide, spacious”): “(you have come to) a wide, welcoming place”.

pitfalls: The ending -an (tanwīn) is pronounced: marḥaban — the alif only carries it.
subtleties: A friendly reply repeats it or answers with أَهْلًا; colloquial Levantine even says مَرْحَبْتَيْن, “two hellos”.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses the interjection أَهْلًا as “hi; welcome” — the greeting “hello” in its everyday form.

profile.feeling: Casual and friendly: “hi!”, and the word that welcomes a guest.

examples.tr: Hi! I am a new student.

etymology.text: Adverbial accusative of أَهْل (ʾahl, “family, kin”): “(you are) among family”. أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا is short for لَقَدْ صَادَفْتُمْ أَهْلًا وَوَطِئْتُمْ سَهْلًا, “you have met your own people and trodden on even ground” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا literally says: “(you have come to) family, and (you tread on) easy ground”.
pitfalls: أَهْلًا وَسَهْلًا is “welcome!” to a guest — not “you’re welcome” after thanks (that is عَفْوًا).
subtleties: It is also the quick answer to مَرْحَبًا: مَرْحَبًا! — أَهْلًا!

profile.feeling: The greeting that works everywhere — street, shop, office, mosque; it carries a blessing.

senses.def: peace be upon you — hello (to one person or many)

examples.tr: Peace be upon you! — And upon you be peace!
He came in and said: “Peace be upon you.”

etymology.text: Literally “the peace (be) upon you (pl.)”; Wiktionary gives it as cognate with Hebrew שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם (shalóm aleikhém).

funFacts: Hebrew שָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיכֶם (shalóm aleikhém) is the same greeting word for word — both from the Semitic root š-l-m, “peace, wholeness”.
Turkish selam and selamünaleyküm come from it.
pitfalls: عَلَيْكُمْ is plural even to one person: it is a fixed formula.
The answer is always وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ — with وَ and a -u before the article.
subtleties: A fuller answer adds blessings: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ وَرَحْمَةُ اللّٰهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ.

lexemes.role: the fixed answer to السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ: “and upon you be peace”

profile.feeling: Bright and polite — the morning greeting, with a fixed answer.

examples.tr: Good morning! — Good morning! (lit. morning of light)

synonyms.nuance: “morning of jasmine” — a warm, playful variant (Egypt)

funFacts: Turkish sabah (morning) and hayır (no; also “good” in hayırlı) are Arabic loans: صَبَاح and خَيْر.
pitfalls: The answer is not the same phrase but صَبَاحُ النُّورِ (morning of light).
subtleties: Used until about noon; later in the day people say مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ.

lexemes.role: the usual answer to صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ: “morning of light”

profile.feeling: Polite and warm — the greeting from the afternoon on.

examples.tr: Good evening! — Good evening! (lit. evening of light)
Good evening, how are you? (to a woman)

pitfalls: It greets when you meet; it is not a goodbye for the night (that is تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ).
The answer is مَسَاءُ النُّورِ.
subtleties: Built like صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ: the same answer pattern with النُّور, “light”.

lexemes.role: the usual answer to مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ: “evening of light”

override.pos: Wiktionary files it as a phrase; in this course fixed formulas are one lexeme with pos INTJ (docs/LANGUAGES.md, multi-word formulas).

profile.feeling: A soft wish at bedtime: “may you wake up to good things”.

examples.text: تُصْبِحُ عَلَى خَيْرٍ! وَأَنْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ.
examples.tr: Good night! — And you too. (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: have a happy night — more formal or written

pitfalls: It is a verb in the 2nd person, so it changes with the listener: to a woman تُصْبِحِينَ عَلَى خَيْرٍ, to several people تُصْبِحُونَ عَلَى خَيْرٍ.
The answer: وَأَنْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ (to a man), وَأَنْتِ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ (to a woman) — “and may you be among its people”.
subtleties: Literally “you wake up upon good”: a wish for the next morning, said when someone goes to bed — not a greeting when you meet in the evening.

profile.feeling: The bedtime wish, said to a woman or a girl.

examples.text: تُصْبِحِينَ عَلَى خَيْرٍ! وَأَنْتَ مِنْ أَهْلِهِ.
examples.tr: Good night! (to a woman) — And you too. (her answer, to a man)

pitfalls: The ending -īna marks “you, a woman”: تُصْبِحِينَ, not تُصْبِحُ.
subtleties: The same ending -īna appears in every present verb addressed to a woman: أَنْتِ تَكُونِينَ.

profile.feeling: The everyday goodbye: “go safely”.

synonyms.nuance: until we meet again — a little more formal

pitfalls: Strictly it is said to the one who leaves; in speech the one leaving often answers اللّٰهُ يُسَلِّمُكَ (may God keep you safe).
subtleties: السَّلَامَة (safety) has the same root س ل م as سَلَام (peace).

profile.feeling: A goodbye with a promise: “until the (next) meeting”.

examples.tr: Goodbye, see you later! (to a man)

synonyms.nuance: goodbye — the most common everyday word

etymology.text: Literally “to the meeting”; a calque of French au revoir (Wiktionary).

funFacts: Russian до свидания is built the same way: “until the meeting” (Wiktionary compares the Slavic calques).
pitfalls: إِلَى is written with alif maqṣūra (ى); before the article its long ā is shortened in speech: ʾila l-liqāʾ.
subtleties: A bit more formal than مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ: typical of TV, radio and the classroom.

profile.feeling: Light and friendly: “see you later”.

examples.tr: See you later at the office.

pitfalls: The “you” follows the listener: أَرَاكَ (man), أَرَاكِ (woman), أَرَاكُمْ (several people).
subtleties: Word for word like English “see you later”: أَرَى “I see” + -ka “you”.

profile.feeling: “See you later”, said to a woman or a girl.

examples.tr: See you later at the university.

etymology.text: From أَرَى (ʾarā, “I see”) + ـكِ (-ki, “you”, feminine) + لَاحِقًا (lāḥiqan, “later”) (Wiktionary).

pitfalls: Only the last vowel of -ki tells it from the masculine: unvocalized both are اراك لاحقا.
subtleties: The same -ki is the “your” of كَيْفَ حَالُكِ and مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.

override.pos: Wiktionary files it as a phrase; in this course fixed formulas are one lexeme with pos INTJ (docs/LANGUAGES.md, multi-word formulas).

profile.feeling: The standard “how are you?” — asked sincerely and often more than once.

senses.def: how are you? (to a man; lit. “how is your state?”)

pitfalls: To a woman: كَيْفَ حَالُكِ (-ki); to several people: كَيْفَ حَالُكُمْ.
Answer with بِخَيْرٍ، شُكْرًا or الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ — and ask back: وَأَنْتَ؟ / وَأَنْتِ؟
subtleties: حَال (state, condition) + -uka (your): Arabic asks about your “state”, not about how you “go” (wie geht’s, как дела).

override.pos: Wiktionary files it as a phrase; in this course fixed formulas are one lexeme with pos INTJ (docs/LANGUAGES.md, multi-word formulas).

profile.feeling: “How are you?”, asked of a woman or a girl.

examples.text: صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ يَا مَرْيَمُ، كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟
examples.tr: Good morning, Maryam, how are you?

pitfalls: Only the last vowel differs from the masculine: حَالُكِ (-ki) vs حَالُكَ (-ka); unvocalized both are كيف حالك.
subtleties: Getting this ending right is how you show you noticed whom you speak to — Arabic marks the listener’s gender everywhere.

override.pos: Wiktionary files بِخَيْرٍ as a prepositional phrase (bi- + ḵayr); it works as a predicate adverbial “well, fine”, so it is ADV here.

profile.feeling: Reassuring: “I’m well, all is good”.

examples.tr: Thank God, we are all fine.

funFacts: خَيْر (good) is also in صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ; Turkish hayır and, through Turkish, Greek χαΐρι (good, benefit) go back to it.
pitfalls: It never changes: أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ، هِيَ بِخَيْرٍ، نَحْنُ بِخَيْرٍ — no gender, no plural.
The ending is tanwīn: bi-ḫayrin; in speech you mostly hear bi-ḫēr.
subtleties: كُلُّ عَامٍ وَأَنْتُمْ بِخَيْرٍ (“every year may you be well”) is the standard wish for a holiday or a birthday.

lexemes.role: the most common answer to كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟ — “praise be to God”, i.e. fine, thank God

override.pos: Wiktionary files it as a phrase; in this course fixed formulas are one lexeme with pos INTJ (docs/LANGUAGES.md, multi-word formulas).

profile.feeling: Gratitude, said by believers and non-believers alike — the usual answer to “how are you?”.

senses.def: praise be to God; thank God — also the answer “fine, thank God”

examples.tr: How are you? — Fine, thank God.

funFacts: It is also the second verse of the Qurʾān (الْحَمْدُ لِلّٰهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ).
pitfalls: As an answer it means “fine (thank God)”, even when things are only so-so — it is not a religious statement in that use.
subtleties: Two words: الْحَمْدُ (the praise) + لِلّٰهِ (to God, with the preposition لِـ joined).

override.pos: Wiktionary has اِسْمِي as a noun form (ism + -ī) and as the phrasebook phrase “my name is …”; here it is the formula, pos INTJ.

profile.feeling: The first sentence of every introduction.

examples.tr: Hello, my name is Layla, and I am a student.

funFacts: Hebrew שְׁמִי (shmi, my name) is the same word: Arabic اِسْم = Hebrew שֵׁם (Proto-Semitic *šim-, Wiktionary).
pitfalls: No verb “is”: اِسْمِي سَارَةُ = my name (is) Sara.
The first alif is a connecting hamza: after another word it is not pronounced — وَاسْمِي (wa-smī).
subtleties: To ask: مَا اسْمُكَ؟ (to a man) / مَا اسْمُكِ؟ (to a woman).

profile.feeling: Courteous and warm: “we are honoured (to meet you)”.

senses.def: nice to meet you (lit. “we have been honoured”)

examples.tr: Nice to meet you! — The honour is mine.
I am a teacher here. Nice to meet you.

synonyms.nuance: “a happy opportunity” — pleased to meet you, often when parting
I was glad to meet you (to a man)

etymology.text: First person plural past of تَشَرَّفَ (tašarrafa, “to be honoured”): “we are honoured” (Wiktionary).

pitfalls: It is a past verb (“we have been honoured”) but means “nice to meet you” now; it does not change for the listener.
subtleties: Usual replies: الشَّرَفُ لِي (the honour is mine) or تَشَرَّفْنَا again.

profile.feeling: Friendly and light: “what a happy chance (to meet you)”.

senses.def: pleased to meet you (lit. “a happy opportunity”)

examples.tr: Pleased to meet you! — I am even happier.
Goodbye — it was nice to meet you!

synonyms.nuance: nice to meet you — “we are honoured”

pitfalls: It is a noun phrase, so it does not change for the listener.
subtleties: Very often said at the end of a first meeting, like “nice to have met you”.

profile.feeling: The plain, universal “thanks”.

collocations.tr: thank you (to a man / a woman)

funFacts: Turkish teşekkür (thanks) comes from Arabic تَشَكُّر, of the same root ش ك ر.
pitfalls: The answer is عَفْوًا (you’re welcome).
subtleties: The -an (tanwīn) is pronounced: šukran; it marks the accusative of a noun used as an adverb, like أَهْلًا and عَفْوًا.

profile.feeling: Modest and polite: “don’t mention it”; as a question, “pardon?”.

examples.tr: You’re welcome — no thanks are needed for a duty.

synonyms.nuance: “no thanks for a duty” — modest and warm

funFacts: Turkish af (pardon) and affedersiniz (excuse me) come from the same Arabic word عَفْو.
pitfalls: One word, three jobs: after thanks “you’re welcome”; as a question “pardon?”; before a request “excuse me”.
subtleties: Literally “(I ask) forgiveness”: Arabic answers thanks by playing the favour down.

profile.feeling: Polite softening: “out of your kindness”.

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the station?

synonyms.nuance: “if you allow” — please, excuse me; also to get attention
please — on notices: رَجَاءً، لَا تُدَخِّنْ

etymology.text: مِنْ (min, “from, out of”) + فَضْل (faḍl, “kindness, favour”) + ـكَ (-ka, “your”): “out of your kindness”.

funFacts: Turkish lütfen (please) is built in the same spirit from another Arabic noun, لُطْف (kindness).
pitfalls: To a woman: مِنْ فَضْلِكِ (-ki); to several people: مِنْ فَضْلِكُمْ.
subtleties: It can stand before or after the request, like English “please”.

profile.feeling: “Please”, said to a woman or a girl.

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the library?

synonyms.nuance: “if you allow” — please, excuse me (to a woman)

etymology.text: مِنْ (min, “from, out of”) + فَضْل (faḍl, “kindness, favour”) + ـكِ (-ki, “your”, feminine).

funFacts: The verb before it changes too: اِجْلِسْ (to a man) → اِجْلِسِي (to a woman) — Arabic marks the listener twice.
pitfalls: Unvocalized it is the same as the masculine (من فضلك); say -ki clearly.
subtleties: Wiktionary lists both forms on one page: مِنْ فَضْلِكَ / مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.

profile.feeling: The standard way to get attention politely — a waiter, a passer-by.

senses.def: excuse me; please (to a man; lit. “if you allowed”)

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the door?

synonyms.nuance: “with your permission” — excuse me, to pass or to leave

pitfalls: To a woman: لَوْ سَمَحْتِ; to several people: لَوْ سَمَحْتُمْ.
It is a past verb after لَوْ (“if you allowed”) but means the present.
subtleties: To get past someone, عَنْ إِذْنِكَ is more natural; لَوْ سَمَحْتَ asks for attention or a favour.

profile.feeling: “Excuse me”, said to a woman.

examples.tr: Excuse me, where is the teacher?
Excuse me! What is your name?

pitfalls: The final -ti (سَمَحْتِ) is the only difference from the masculine -ta.
subtleties: The same -ti ending marks “you (woman)” in every past verb: كُنْتِ (you were).

profile.feeling: A sincere apology; it agrees with the one who apologises.

examples.tr: I am very sorry. (a man speaking)
We are sorry for the delay.

synonyms.nuance: sorry, pardon — does not change with the speaker

etymology.text: Derived from the active participle of the verb أَسِفَ (ʔasifa, “to regret, to grieve”) (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The same root gives أَسَف (regret): لِلْأَسَفِ / مَعَ الْأَسَفِ = unfortunately.
pitfalls: It agrees with the speaker: a man says آسِفٌ, a woman آسِفَةٌ, men آسِفُونَ, women آسِفَاتٌ.
For condolences Arabic uses fixed formulas (الْبَقَاءُ لِلّٰهِ) rather than آسِف.
subtleties: أَنَا آسِفٌ is a verbless sentence: “I (am) regretful” — the present “am” is not said.

profile.feeling: A short, polite “sorry / pardon”.

examples.tr: Excuse me, is this your seat?

synonyms.nuance: sorry — agrees with the speaker (آسِفٌ / آسِفَةٌ)

pitfalls: Unlike آسِف it never changes for the speaker.
subtleties: Literally “(I ask) an excuse”; common in writing and on signs: عُذْرًا، الْمَحَلُّ مُغْلَقٌ.

profile.feeling: Clear and polite; as a question (نَعَمْ؟) it answers a call.

senses.def: yes? (answering when called; asking someone to go on)

examples.text: — هَلْ أَنْتَ جَاهِزٌ؟ — نَعَمْ، أَنَا جَاهِزٌ.

examples.tr: Yes, I’d like coffee without sugar.
He said yes to the offer.

synonyms.nuance: yes, indeed — more formal or literary
yes (on the contrary) — the answer that contradicts a negative question

etymology.text: Wiktionary links it to the root ن ع م (“to be pleased, to live in comfort”), cognate with Hebrew נָעַם (naʿam, “to please”).

funFacts: Hebrew נָעִים (naʿim, “pleasant”) — as in נָעִים מְאוֹד, “nice to meet you” — comes from the same Semitic root.
pitfalls: To a negative question, “yes, it is so” is بَلَى, not نَعَمْ: أَلَيْسَ هٰذَا بَصَلًا؟ — بَلَى (Isn’t this onion? — Yes, it is). نَعَمْ would confirm the negative.
Unvocalized نعم can also be نِعْمَ (“how excellent …!”) or نَعَم (cattle) — the vowels and the final sukūn of نَعَمْ tell them apart.
subtleties: Said as a question, نَعَمْ؟ means “yes? / pardon?”; with a sharp tone it can sound like “excuse me?!”.

override.meaning: Wiktionary glosses لَا as “no, not”; the answer “no” is that sense (the word “no” is too short for the automatic gloss match).

profile.feeling: A plain “no”; in hospitality, often said once and then overruled by the host.

phrases.tr: no, and a thousand times no

synonyms.nuance: no, by no means — an emphatic rejection, frequent in the Qurʾān

etymology.text: Inherited from Proto-Semitic *lā; compare Hebrew לֹא (lo).

funFacts: Hebrew לֹא (lo) is the same Proto-Semitic word *lā — and it also means both “no” and “not”.
pitfalls: The answer “no” and the negation “not” are the same written word لَا (separate words in this course). As an answer it stands alone, usually followed by a comma; as negation it stands directly before a present verb: لَا أُحِبُّ.
subtleties: A first لَا to food or drink is often not taken as final in Arab hospitality — the host may insist; a firm refusal usually repeats it with thanks: لَا، شُكْرًا.
